newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian march for jobs demands social Europe.
newsitem.headline: Belgian march for jobs demands social Europe.

text.p: Tens of thousands of trades unionists and politicians from all over Europe marched through Brussels on Sunday to vent their anger at high unemployment and the steady erosion of job security.

"Today's demonstration is not the end. It is not the final act. Together united we will continue our struggle for a social Europe. For a Europe of solidarity," Michel Nollet, head of Belgium's Communist FGTB union, told the colourful, noisy crowd.

Unions expected 60,000 people to turn up from all over Europe for a March for Jobs sparked off by the shock announcement two weeks ago that French carmaker Renault was closing its Belgian Vilvoorde plant with the loss of 3,100 jobs.
The crowd was awash with colour and noise -- red and green union banners and balloons, ear-shattering whistles and firecrackers, chanting, sirens and megaphones.
A hanging effigy of Renault Chairman Louis Schweitzer was prominent among the banners, one of which called him "the shame of Europe".
More than 500 police and 1,000 gendarmes were on the streets along the three kilometre (1.8 mile) route linking Brussels's north and south railway stations. Medical teams were on standby.

"What Renault did was disgusting. We did our best. We did everything they asked for," said Vilvoorde worker Jan De Koninck, 33. "Perhaps for Vilvoorde it is too late but we are now starting something to change the situation in Europe."

Unemployment, a seeping sore as the 15 European Union nations slash their budgets and raise taxes in the struggle to ready their economies for joining the bloc's single currency in 1999, has become a uniting force.
"This is a symbolic demonstration in the heart of the capital of Europe," French Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin told Reuters as he joined the march.
"We need a better balance in the European economic and social model. It has gone too far in liberalisation. Social, not just economic constraints, have to be taken into account."
News of the Renault closure came on top of the bankruptcy in January of Belgian steelmaker Forges de Clabecq, threatening another 1,800 jobs.
Unions said there were thousands of workers from France, and delegations from Spain, Portugal, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Italy, Greece, Austria, Hungary, Slovenia and the Czech Republic.
"It is a show of solidarity. We are all workers. We are all in the struggle," said Stewart Davis, 22, who came with a delegation from the Rolls Royce plant at Bristol in Britain.
"We are here to express our solidarity with the workers of Belgium," Manuel Zaguirre Cano, a spanish union official said. "We have to fight on the European level."
Newspapers reported that Renault sales in Belgium had fallen 40 percent since the news of the closure.
Unemployment in the 15-nation European Union is stuck at 10.8 percent of the workforce, with most governments apparently unable to tackle the looming social crisis.

The unions want consultations with employers on issues such as working hours, and for governments to cut the indirect tax costs of employment and introduce tax policies that encourage jobs, a coherent social policy and moves to encourage economic growth instead of budget belt tightening.
EU social affairs ministers who met in Rotterdam at the weekend said there should be a clear code of conduct for multinationals both opening and closing factories.
But with the decision day on who will be in the vanguard of nations joining the EU's single currency less than a year away, countries are tightening their belts in a bid to join the club.
